newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Old machinery threat to Yugoslav farming recovery.
newsitem.headline: Old machinery threat to Yugoslav farming recovery.

text.p: Agriculture experts warned on Tuesday that unless money is found to update Yugoslavia's run down farm machinery, the sector's recovery would be seriously threatened.

"Agriculture, unlike other industries, has used its capacities and machinery under the sanction years and now they are worn out," Ratko Nikolic, director of the Institute for Agricultural Mechanisation of Novi Sad told Reuters.
According to Nikolic, outdated machinery cuts average yields by 10-15 percent, raises fuel consumption by 20 percent and increases production costs by 30-40 percent.
"We simply cannot afford this. Our priority must be to overhaul old machinery," he said.
Out of around 6.2 million hectares of agricultural land in Yugoslavia, which comprises Serbia and Montenegro, 4.8 million ha is arable land.
The country has some 418,000 agricultural tractors, 250,000 multi-cultivators and 24,000 combines.
"The number of machines is sufficient but the state they are in is not," Nikolic said.
Tractors, which are on average between 12 (in the socially owned sector) to 17 (on private farms) years old, are operating at the level of 30-40 percent of their capacity.

The country needs around 20,000 additional tractors, 16,000-18,000 combines and 25,000-30,000 pieces of other agricultural equipment each year by the year 2000 to return to the pre-war 1990 production level.
"Out of total number of tractors needed, at least 300-400 heavy ones (200 horse power each) should be imported annually by the year 2000," Nikolic said.
But analysts doubt the plan would be achieved considering empty state coffers and overall cash shortage in the economy.
The country's tractor industry, with its pre-sanctions annual capacity of some 45,000 small and medium-size tractors, last year produced barely 1,600 units.

"The only way round the existing outer wall of sanctions which bars the country's access to foreign funds is to directly conclude deals with foreign partners," said Mirko Martinovic of the country's largest agricultural corporation Poljoprivredni kombinat Beograd (PKB).
PKB recently bought 20 heavy Massey Ferguson tractors worth $2.3 billion. Massey Ferguson (a unit of LucasVarity ) offered a five-year credit line with one year grace period.
"We can pay it back either in cash or the equivalent in agricultural products," Martinovic said.
Industry sources saw the deal as a good start to eliminate bottlenecks in the country's agriculture.
"We have paved the way for other domestic companies that are interested in establishing similar cooperation with foreign partners," said Stanko Stankovski, marketing director of PKB.
According to some estimates, a total of about 400,000 tractors must be overhauled to be ready for the ambitious spring campaign planned on over 2.3 million ha. -- Belgrade Newsroom ++381 11 222 4254
